case40v1-req.edge.cases:
Vyuha Systems and the States Nobody Specified

A field-force platform built in Pune has sold three permissions its device token has no room for. Pune, Bengaluru, Berlin, Toronto, Singapore, Edison and Dubai, November 2026.

Sunday night, Kalyani Nagar

At eleven on the night of Sunday 22 November 2026, Gaganjot Magotra sat at her kitchen table in Kalyani Nagar, Pune, with four windows open. In twelve hours she would tell Vyuha Systems' chief executive which of four plans would own the engineering capacity from December to February, and on 2 December defend it to a board promised the Gulf.

The first window held an email from Dubai, sent at 9.30 that evening local time by Gurbani Mahil, head of store systems at Rawdha Retail Group, on a Sunday, not a working day in the Emirates either. It asked one question: whether the supervisor override demonstrated in September would be in the 15 January build. The second was a Bengaluru thread in which her head of engineering had written that the handset permission field had two bits free. The third was a Toronto dashboard, refreshed at 12.30 that afternoon Eastern, showing that in October a third of field sessions had not completed on a live connection. The fourth was a comment her designer in Berlin had left on the board pre-read at 6.30 p.m. CET and that Magotra had not answered.

She had been a product manager eleven years and had never had a quarter in which four plans sat this far apart in cost.

A company shaped by one compression decision

Vyuha Systems Private Limited was founded in Pune in August 2017 to put a reliable order-capture app on the cheap Android handsets India's distribution salesmen carry. Its first enterprise contract, signed in March 2019 with a decorative-paints distributor network in Maharashtra, set the pattern it still sells: an offline-first handset client, a web console for supervisors, and a sync layer it calls the ledger. By November 2026 it served 41 enterprise clients, 38,400 monthly active field users in India, and annual recurring revenue of ₹58.2 crore against ₹47.6 crore of revenue in the year to March 2026.

The decision that constrains everything today was made in August 2022 and was then obviously right. To hold sync payloads under the 2G and 3G ceilings its users lived with, Gurkirat Moudgil packed the whole permission model into a sixteen-bit mask inside the device token. Sixteen capabilities, one word, no round trip. Changing that field's shape means a schema migration and a forced handset upgrade — and in October 2026, 31 per cent of devices in the India base ran an operating system the current store build no longer auto-updates. A second decision, in June 2023, let each client define its own sequence of outlet-visit states. It won deals. It also means the 41 clients now run 19 distinct state machines, and Vyuha's requirements template has no section in which states are written down.

The industry around it

India's retail-execution software market sits between two pressures. Above it are the platforms that have made distribution legible — Reliance Retail's and Flipkart's supply systems, ONDC's rails, Meesho's reseller economics — and the Indian software firms that set buyers' expectations: Zoho, Freshworks, Postman. Below it are the realities of the route: a salesman on a Jio or Airtel connection in a tier-3 town, a kirana owner who gives him ninety seconds, GST e-invoicing deadlines indifferent to coverage, and UPI collection flows NPCI keeps tightening. The DPDP Act's consent and access obligations have made every permission question a legal one too, and clients now ask who inside their own organisation may see a route, a margin field or a rep's location history.

Vyuha's exposure is no longer domestic. Its Singapore office covers South-East Asia; its Gulf pipeline, opened by the Rawdha contract of 2 October 2026, is worth ₹14.2 crore over three years, ₹4.1 crore of it in the first year. Rawdha's agreement requires store-level personal data to remain on infrastructure inside the UAE, which Vyuha serves from a small Dubai-region instance that cannot be folded into its Mumbai region.

What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Sehatkar Pharmacies, a chain in fourteen cities, went live on 12 January 2026 with 5,210 field users and a visit state machine of its own. In April its area managers began raising what the support queue came to call ghost orders: orders a rep swore he had taken that nobody at head office could find, and duplicates of orders that had in fact arrived. The working theory through April, May and June was connectivity, reasonably enough: Sehatkar's worst districts are exactly where coverage drops, and the ledger's retry logic had never been instrumented.

On 1 July 2026 a telemetry build shipped from Toronto, defining eleven named session end-states and recording whether the handset had a live connection when each session ended. October 2026 was the first clean month on the taxonomy and is reproduced as Exhibit 1. Of the 39,300 sessions that ended at a permission block, 23,900 — 60.8 per cent — had a live connection when the block fired. Moudgil believes the blocks are the handset re-checking a cached token against a role a supervisor had changed in the web console, with no screen designed for the result.

Exhibit 3 sets these events against the decisions that preceded them. Two further beliefs have since failed. The mask was expected in 2022 to last a decade; Exhibit 2 shows the last two bits allocated in March 2026, forty-three months after the design, to client-specific features used by two clients and by one. And the reconciliation in Exhibit 4, produced in Singapore from client ERP extracts for the July–September quarter, counts orders never received at all — a different population from Exhibit 1's abandoned sessions, over a different window, from a different source.

The people

Gaganjot Magotra, vice-president of product, Pune. Holds that the quarter must buy a permission model Vyuha can sell twice, not once. Her incentive is a product organisation she has argued should own specification. She has not told anyone that she signed off the Rawdha demo script in September without reading the token schema.

Gurmeet Manhas, co-founder and chief executive, Pune. Holds that the Gulf contract is the only credible path to a Series C and must ship on 15 January. His incentive is a round he has been sounding out since August. He has not said that two of his three term sheets name Rawdha in their diligence lists.

Gurkirat Moudgil, head of engineering, Bengaluru. Holds that the ledger and the token are the only reason Vyuha works on a ₹6,000 handset, and that a rewrite in one quarter is fantasy. His incentive is a platform he designed and whose conflict-resolution code he still owns. He has not said he learned of bits 15 and 16 on 17 November.

Goutam Mengi, data scientist, Toronto. Holds that nothing can be decided until the eleven end-states are measured per client rather than in aggregate. His incentive is an instrumentation roadmap promised for three quarters. He has not said the fourteen-day log retention was his own cost saving, proposed in May.

Gitasri Mahendru, principal designer, Berlin. Holds that the company has never written down what a state is, and that screens for empty, offline, first-run and admin states cannot be designed client by client. Her incentive is a design system she cannot ship against 19 state machines. She has not said she has been interviewing since September.

Gowri Mutneja, customer-success lead, Singapore. Holds that Sehatkar's renewal on 31 January is the larger number and the nearer cliff. Her incentive is a gross-revenue-retention target across her book. She has not said that Sehatkar's chief operating officer has already asked her, informally, what migrating off Vyuha would involve.

Gunbir Makkar, head of sales, Edison, New Jersey. Holds that the Gulf and then North America are where the multiple is, and that engineering has had the Gulf requirements since July. His incentive is an accelerator triggering on Rawdha's first-year value. He has not said the July proposal called the supervisor override “configurable today”.

Voices

“Gaganjot, I will be straight. My board asks me on Tuesday whether override is in the build. I do not need the architecture. I need yes or no, and I need it true this time.”

Gurbani Mahil, Rawdha Retail Group, email, 22 November 2026, 9.30 p.m. GST

“Three new capabilities is three bits. We have two free. Worst case we take bit 12 back — nine clients export outlet lists, and they can do it from the console.”

Gurkirat Moudgil, engineering channel, 11 November 2026

“Eight hundred and twenty-seven lakh in one quarter. Annualise it: thirty-three crore of our clients' order value out of the door, against fifty-eight crore of ARR. Tell me again this is a backlog item.”

Gunbir Makkar, pipeline review thread, 17 November 2026

“Twelve thousand four hundred were duplicates, and a cancelled duplicate is not a lost order. Nobody has shown me those two exhibits measuring the same thing.”

Gitasri Mahendru, same thread, 17 November 2026

“The ERP view sees only submitted orders. An abandoned session submits nothing, so Exhibit 4 is a floor on a different quantity. Give me ninety days of state logs per client and I will tell you which.”

Goutam Mengi, call with Magotra, 18 November 2026

“Every option buys a different way of shipping permissions. None tells me what a state is, or who decides a screen for an empty admin view exists. We will be back here in April.”

Gitasri Mahendru, comment on the board pre-read, 22 November 2026

The options as Magotra sees them

The four plans were drafted on the board's investment template, which asks for a deliverable, a cost in engineer-weeks and a cash figure; Exhibit 5 is that page. Exhibit 6 sets each option's demand against the window's capacity: of its 108 engineer-weeks, 34 are committed to the UAE residency build and a GST e-invoicing change, leaving 74.

Option A, the state layer. One state machine for all clients, the eleven end-states made explicit, a generated screen for each, and a token re-check on role change. It replaces the sixteen-bit mask with a variable-length grant list and requires a forced handset upgrade. It leaves the ledger's conflict resolution and the Dubai-region instance as they are.

Option B, three bits. Extend the token by one word to carry the three Rawdha capabilities, ship the override, the on-device audit view and session suspension, and leave the taxonomy, the 19 state machines and the empty-state screens as they are. It requires a forced handset upgrade for clients taking the new word.

Option C, see first. Per-client instrumentation of the eleven end-states, a four-person triage squad for the quarter, and the design system's empty, offline, first-run and admin screens specified but not built. No new permission capability ships in the window.

Option D, buy the model. Licence an external policy service, move authorisation off the device token, keep a cached deny-by-default grant for offline use. It requires a second instance inside the UAE to satisfy Rawdha's residency clause and leaves the taxonomy untouched.

The deadline and the hard constraints

Rawdha's go-live is 15 January 2027. The agreement carries service credits of ₹18 lakh a week from that date, capped at ₹1.8 crore, ten weeks' worth. Sehatkar's renewal falls on 31 January and is worth ₹6.3 crore of annual recurring revenue; its contract requires a written remediation plan by 15 December. The board has approved ₹200 lakh of discretionary product spend for the quarter. Nine engineers can touch the handset client; Moudgil alone has worked on the ledger's conflict resolution, and his fortnight in Jammu falls inside the shutdown the 108-engineer-week figure already excludes. Contract engineers cost ₹2.10 lakh a week, so covering Option A's gap with 72 bought weeks is ₹151.2 lakh on top of ₹99.9 lakh of internal time, ₹251.1 lakh in all, and Moudgil puts ledger onboarding at six weeks. The DPDP Act's access provisions and Rawdha's residency clause both bear on where an audit trail may sit.

Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 1 reports end-states for one month, and Magotra must quote the board one number on 2 December. Should its denominator be sessions, users, outlets visited or orders submitted — and what does each choice conceal?
  2. Exhibit 2 records when each bit was allocated and how many clients use it. What does that pattern reveal about how Vyuha decides what a permission is, and what would you need to know before allocating a seventeenth?
  3. Exhibits 1 and 4 come from different sources over different windows. What may each legitimately be used to claim on its own, and which claims require both?
  4. Mengi, Moudgil, Mahendru and Makkar each read the record differently. Which of their claims can be tested against evidence that exists on 22 November, and which cannot be tested at all?
  5. Magotra has framed Monday as a choice among four engineering investments. What decision would a different framing put in front of her, and which evidence here would that framing make central that the present one makes irrelevant?
  6. It is Monday morning, 23 November. What do you do in the first week, and in what order — and what exactly do you tell the board on 2 December about the Rawdha commitment, Sehatkar's renewal and the state of the product? What would have to be true for you to be wrong?

Later that night

Magotra read the template's three fields again — deliverable, engineer-weeks, cash — and then Mahendru's comment, a fourth time. She typed a reply, deleted it, typed a shorter one. Outside, a delivery rider idled at the gate with his phone held against the wall for signal. Mahil's email still sat unanswered, and it was now a quarter past midnight on Monday.
exp40v2-req.edge.cases:
Edge cases, states and permissions

Empty, loading, failed, offline, first-run, denied, admin. Every practitioner can recite it. The question is why competent teams keep shipping surfaces with four of them.

1Two decisions, seventeen days apart

On Monday 14 September 2026 the month-end close across Goshwara Systems' forty-one lender clients came up 1,180 approvals short. Goshwara, a Pune firm, sells a credit-operations console to non-banking financial companies; 1,240 named users live in it. A fortnight earlier Navroop Yohal, who runs product, had signed off a least-privilege migration collapsing 63 roles to 11, on Monday 31 August. The policy was right in principle and over-removed; the screen was worse. Users whose entitlement had been withdrawn saw no refusal, but the queue picker's report, in the grey type it keeps for an idle Tuesday: You have no queues assigned. On audit, 1,096 of the 1,412 role assignments (77.6 per cent) kept all they had held; the other 316 lost at least one permission. Those 316 belonged to 274 users, 22.1 per cent of the 1,240 seats, of whom 59 raised a ticket.

On Thursday 1 October, in Rajkot, Nimrat Yamotra was arguing about a sentence. Gagar Water Systems has 2.6 lakh connected reverse-osmosis purifiers in Indian homes, and its app is about to show filter life. At any moment 1.9 per cent of that base, 4,940 units, has not reached Gagar's servers for over seven days. Naunidh Yamla, her platform lead, wants a default: estimate from the last known flow total. Yamotra wants a state: filter life unknown, last contact nine days ago. If the default is wrong and a filter has expired, warranty exposure at ₹1,450 a replacement is 4,940 × ₹1,450 = ₹71.63 lakh — the ceiling if every unreachable filter had expired.

These are one argument. In both products a negative answer and an absent answer reach the renderer looking identical, and it cannot separate them.

2What the idea is, and who disagrees about it

Take one surface: a screen, route or component with its own data dependency. A state of it is an equivalence class of situations it renders differently — tuples of row count, fetch status, whether the network reached this endpoint, whether the account has been here before, and what the policy layer permits this subject to do. An edge case is a class with small mass and large consequence. Permissions are not a state but a relation over subjects and objects, decided elsewhere, which induces states; collapsing the two is the most productive single error here.

The lineage is old. Mealy and Moore gave the finite-state machine its canonical forms in 1955 and 1956; Harel's statecharts, in 1987, added hierarchy, orthogonality and broadcast; orthogonality is the import that matters, since independent dimensions multiply rather than add. Myers supplied the sampling discipline in 1979 as equivalence partitioning and boundary-value analysis; Nielsen's 1994 heuristics made visibility of status and error recovery evaluable — when the empty state became an artefact somebody owned. The authorisation line runs parallel: Lampson's access matrix (1971), Harrison, Ruzzo and Ullman proving general safety undecidable (1976), role-based access control (Ferraiolo and Kuhn 1992; NIST 2004), attribute-based access control (NIST SP 800-162, 2014) and Zanzibar (2019). All of it closes one gap: between what a feature does and what a screen does in every configuration it can reach.

Four schools disagree, not about whether empty states matter. The enumerative school signs: the designed state set is finite, derivable before code from the cross-product of orthogonal dimensions, and reviewable; it will not sign that a state which never occurred was never a defect. The empirical school signs: the mass distribution over states is unknowable in advance, so observability is the cheaper half of the budget; it will not sign that an unobserved state deserves a design. The invariant school signs: a total renderer, degrading rather than branching, needs fewer designed states; it will not sign that every state deserves bespoke copy. The policy school signs: a decision taken outside the policy layer is a defect even when correct; it will not sign that admin is a state.

3Mechanics: the cross-product, and the quotient

The procedure has two movements. The first is mechanical: list the orthogonal dimensions, and multiply. Goshwara's approvals queue, on Monday 6 October 2025, looked like this.

Table 1. Orthogonal dimensions of Goshwara's approvals queue.
DimensionValuesCount
Row count0; 1–9; 10–499; 500+4
Fetchpending; success; failed3
Linkconnected; offline with cache2
Authorisationnone; viewer; approver; admin4

4 × 3 × 2 × 4 = 96 cells. The team's own estimate that morning was four states: ideal, loading, error, empty.

Ninety-six is the figure usually produced to prove enumeration impossible, and proves nothing of the kind: almost all those cells render identically. The second movement is to quotient the space: find the classes the renderer can distinguish. No entitlement absorbs the rest, so the 24 cells where authorisation is none become one screen: 96 to 73. A pending or failed fetch makes the row count unobservable, so within each remaining level eight pending cells collapse to two and eight failed to two: 73 to 37. On success, connected and offline-with-cache differ by a staleness banner rather than a page, so eight success cells per level become four: 37 to 25. Finally the three remaining levels share the pending and failed classes, viewer and approver share the empty one, and approver merges with admin wherever their row controls match, leaving 13.

Only the third reduction is a design decision; the others say what the renderer can express. It asserts that staleness is chrome, not a state. Reverse it — a treasury user reconciling a cut-off needs stale data visibly distinct — and the success block carries both link values through: four empty classes and twelve populated instead of two and six, so the designed set rises from 13 to 21.

Three steps are left implicit. Reachability: some cells are impossible rather than redundant, and an enumeration that cannot say which over-builds. Transitions: thirteen nodes admit 13 × 12 = 156 ordered transitions, almost all irrelevant and one not — permit to deny while a draft is unsaved. Persistence: which state survives a reload.

Permissions have their own arithmetic, and it is compression. The console defines 86 permissions; assigning them directly to 1,240 seats is 1,240 × 86 = 106,640 cell-level decisions to keep correct. With nine roles and one per seat it is 1,240 user–role assignments plus 9 × 86 = 774 role–permission edges, a total of 2,014: 106,640 / 2,014 = 52.9 times fewer. That is the case for roles, and it decays.

By August 2026 the console carried 63 roles and 1,412 user–role assignments, some seats holding two: 1,412 + 63 × 86 = 6,830 decisions against 2,014 at launch, a factor of 3.39 over fourteen months on an unchanged population. Worse, 41 of the 63 roles (65.1 per cent) were held by exactly one user: access-matrix rows wearing a role's clothes. The diagnostic is the singleton share, with the honest caveat that no threshold for it is established in the literature.

4When the discipline applies, and when it misleads

Three claims decide whether the exercise earns its cost, all testable in advance. One: the surface has two or more orthogonal dimensions the user cannot control. Goshwara's queue has connectivity and entitlement; Gagar's card has device liveness and telemetry age. Both pass. A settings screen whose only input is the user's typing fails, which is why such screens rarely reward it. Two: a wrong render in a low-mass state costs more than designing it. Goshwara's telemetry, in section 8, shows cost per occurrence varying 762-fold; Gagar's is a ₹71.63 lakh ceiling on 1.9 per cent of the base. Three: authorisation is decided in exactly one place. Where it is not, the exercise misleads, because the matrix you enumerate is not the one that ships. Goshwara failed it: nine checks lived in view code.

Two situations make the idea mislead rather than waste effort. A thin projection of an unbounded stream has no terminal states, so enumerating yields a taxonomy of moments; and a surface due for rewrite in six weeks turns the enumeration into inventory.

5Hard edges: seams, regulation, devices, models

In a multi-product company the state belongs to the composition, not to any component: entitlement to product A with none to B produces a cross-sell shell no team owns, renders or sees. Two-sided products are sharper: the forgotten state is the other side's emptiness and a supply-side zero renders on the demand side as a failure. A rider shown something went wrong instead of no driver has accepted yet has a wrong state.

Regulation turns states into obligations and removes the freedom to collapse them. Under the Reserve Bank of India's account aggregator framework a lapsed consent is a distinct, loggable condition; under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 so is a withdrawn one. Both render as no data; neither may be designed as it.

Hardware is where the category error is hardest to see. A device has states the application cannot observe, and absent telemetry is a state of the link, not of the device — Gagar's whole dispute in one sentence. The state set is the union over every firmware version in the field: Gagar supports four trains, so a card correct on the newest has three other renderings to get right. AI-native products invert it: a model does not return empty, it returns something. Emptiness becomes a confidence state, continuous rather than discrete, plus the refusal and the stale index.

What mature companies do, rather than what their process documents claim, is rarely to keep a state matrix in a PRD. It is to put the obligation in the component library: a list primitive that cannot be instantiated without its empty, denied and stale slots filled in. A matrix must be remembered; a primitive is a compile-time error.

6Eight distinctions that separate the expert

A denial that renders as an absence. The tell-tale is a ticket saying the list is empty beside a log showing the query never ran, or ran with a filter that could return nothing. A data bug is the obvious reading, and wrong: the list is correctly empty for an inadmissible reason.

Loading is not one state. The tell-tale is one spinner with no branch on elapsed time. At an illustrative median of 240 milliseconds a spinner is noise; at a 99th percentile of eleven seconds it wants an escape. One skeleton seems to suffice because latency is imagined as spread; it is bimodal.

Empty has two parents. Never had any and had some and now has none are different designs: onboarding, and a loss event that may need an undo. The tell-tale is get started by adding your first… in front of a six-month-old account — zero rows, true of the data and false of the user.

Offline is a spectrum, and the middle hurts. The tell-tale is a product that handles aeroplane mode and fails on wi-fi that resolves DNS then times out on the handshake. A device-level flag is the obvious reading, and wrong: reachability belongs to an endpoint, not a handset.

First-run is a state of the account, not the installation. The tell-tale is a tutorial shown to a three-year customer who changed handsets. A local flag is cheap and wrong; the honest implementation asks the server whether this subject ever finished.

Admin is not the top of a ladder; it is a different product. The tell-tale is an admin area with no empty states and no error copy, its builders its only users. Configure, impersonate, audit and repair have no analogue below, and impersonation reaches a state no role can.

Role explosion is a measurement, not a mood. The tell-tale is the singleton share — 41 of 63 roles at Goshwara. Poor hygiene is the obvious reading, and wrong: singletons mean the model's dimensions are wrong, the exception being an attribute wearing a role's name.

The state that matters is often the transition. The tell-tale is a denied state with no your access changed while you were working state. Designing nodes fails wherever a trust boundary moves mid-session, which is what a least-privilege migration does — and why Goshwara's incident was invisible.

7Across product types and company stages

The differences are real in five places and overstated everywhere else. In consumer products mass dominates: empty and first-run states carry the acquisition funnel, and a bad one shows up in day-seven return within a fortnight. In B2B and enterprise authorisation dominates and empty states are rarer, since data arrives by import; the dangerous state is partial entitlement. Goshwara's console has eleven independently permissioned home-screen sections, giving 211 = 2,048 possible layouts, of which exactly 17 occurred in the 92 days from 1 May to 31 July 2026.

Platforms and marketplaces add cross-side emptiness and the API, a surface nobody designs states for, with rate-limited, deprecated-version and partially-authorised responses no screen shows. Hardware adds the link-versus-device distinction; AI products replace emptiness with confidence. Two asserted differences are not real: a loading state is engineered alike everywhere, and offline handling is no consumer speciality.

Stage changes the answer more than type does. At seed, enumeration is inventory and the invariant approach wins outright. Once a product has several teams the state set outgrows memory and only a component contract scales. In a regulated or listed company states become contractual and cannot be deleted.

8Three worked examples

One: the ladder, applied. Goshwara shipped all 13 states in October 2025 against a whiteboard estimate of four. Over the 90 days from 1 November 2025 to 29 January 2026 the surface logged 182,400 sessions and 213 support contacts. Nine of the thirteen occurred and four never did; four of the nine were the whiteboard's.

Table 2. Goshwara approvals queue, 1 November 2025 – 29 January 2026: the eight of thirteen designed states that occurred.
StateSessionsShare of sessions ContactsContacts per 1,000 sessions
Success, 10–499 rows, acting role159,96587.7%240.15
Success, 1–9 rows, acting role8,1904.5%20.24
Success, empty, viewer or approver7,6544.2%91.18
Pending, connected3,1061.7%20.64
Failed, connected1,7441.0%4727.0
Success, 10–499 rows, viewer7290.4%6285.0

Total / pooled182,400100.0%2131.17

The Total row's last cell is the pooled rate, 213 / 182,400 × 1,000 = 1.17, not the column mean. The four that never occurred were a pending fetch while offline, a failed fetch while offline, a 500-plus row count under a viewer role, and an empty queue under an admin; the first two are unreachable, since a cached list is neither pending nor failed.

Two readings of the table are both correct, and they are this field's live disagreement. Cost per occurrence runs from 0.15 to 114.3 contacts per thousand sessions, a factor of 762, strongly inverse to volume: the rank correlation is about −0.88 and the four costliest states sit 5th, 6th, 7th and 9th of nine by traffic. That 114.3 rests on 4 contacts in 35 sessions, the table's least reliable cell. Equally, two of the thirteen were designed and never seen, and two more were unreachable.

Two: a first-run state, tested properly. Gagar ran its rebuilt first-run screen for fourteen days: 4,812 control first runs, 4,790 treatment. Day-seven return was 1,106 / 4,812 = 22.98 per cent against 1,214 / 4,790 = 25.34 per cent, a gain of 2.36 points. The standard error of that difference is the square root of (0.2298 × 0.7702 / 4,812) + (0.2534 × 0.7466 / 4,790), or 0.87 points, so the gain is 2.70 standard errors and Yamotra took it as real. What she refused to conclude matters more. Within the treatment arm 383 first runs happened with the device unreachable and 95 returned: 24.80 per cent, against 25.39 per cent for the other 4,407. That gap of 0.59 points sits against a standard error of 2.30 points — 0.26 of a standard error — and is no evidence that offline first-runs convert worse. Note the contrast: the subgroup against the rest of its own arm, not an arm total containing it.

Three: the migration that failed. Goshwara's migration was right in principle, over-removing in practice, and wrong as a product change, for the reason this page exists to teach: no new state was added, so no telemetry could exist, so the failure was undetectable from the screen's own telemetry. The approvals queue had been through the ladder; the queue picker never had.

Seven of the console's 34 workflow queues, 20.6 per cent, had all their approvers inside the 274 affected users. Across the fourteen blind days the clients created 5,840 approval requests, of which 1,180 (20.2 per cent) landed in those seven queues and were never opened. The diagnostic existed before the change and nobody ran it: a per-assignment diff of lost permissions. Recovery ran to Saturday 19 September: 316 assignments reviewed, 248 restored in full, 68 left reduced because the migration had been right about those.

9Failure modes and their early diagnostics

The third column matters most: a diagnostic question beats a checklist item, since someone who has not read the code can ask it.

Table 3. Five failure modes, their earliest sign, and the cost of catching them late.
Failure modeEarly signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Denial renders as absenceTickets attach empty-state screenshotsCan the log tell a refused read from a zero-row read?Silent stoppage: 1,180 requests in 14 days
One loading design, bimodal latencyp99 over twenty times the median; one spinnerWhat does this screen do at second ten?Abandonment logged as disinterest
Empty state built for the wrong parentOnboarding copy inside a churn cohortNever-had-any, or had-some-and-lost-it?Reactivation read as a welcome
Offline detected per deviceClean in aeroplane mode, broken on captive wi-fiWhich endpoint was unreachable, for how long?Lost writes; lost field collections
Authorisation decided in the viewTwo screens disagree on one entitlementHow many places decide this, and which wins?Audit finding, then re-architecture

10Where experts genuinely disagree

Enumerate first, or instrument first. The enumerative case rests on Table 2: cost per occurrence varies 762-fold and runs strongly inverse to volume, about −0.88 by rank, so discovery ordered by traffic finds the costliest states late — in a money-moving product, after an audit. It would be wrong if cost per occurrence were flat, in which case volume ranking is optimal. The empirical case rests on the other half of the table: four of thirteen states never occurred in 90 days, and two of those four were unreachable by construction, so the enumeration both wasted design and mis-specified reachability.

Is a denial an error or a state? The HTTP tradition answers error: a 403 is a failure, it belongs in the error rate, and that rate should trend to zero. The product tradition answers state: refusals are expected traffic in any multi-tenant system and belong in a traffic-share chart somebody designs for. Goshwara's denial rate was 0.3 per cent of sessions; as an error rate it would have tripped an alert and been engineered away by over-granting. The error view wins wherever most denials are genuine faults rather than correct refusals.

Does the matrix belong in the PRD? Technology-specialist programmes treat the PRD and state matrix as signature artefacts, on the ground that a manager who cannot write the matrix cannot referee the third reduction. The strategy-memo tradition answers that the matrix is an engineering artefact and that a PRD containing it displaces the argument about why. This is unsettled, partly a question about who reads the document.

11What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this asks what does this render when the answer is no before what the feature does, and writes the denied and empty copy first, as the surface's hardest writing. They will not accept the word “offline” without a named endpoint and a duration. They instrument state names rather than error counts, count singleton roles, and say out loud which of the thirteen states they are not building, and why.

12Decisions, and three questions

Three questions first. Goshwara's 762-fold cost spread rests on 213 contacts across nine states: at what sample size would you let that ranking set a design budget, and what would you measure instead with a tenth as many, about 21? Second, construct the strongest case for Yamla's default, and name the evidence that would decide. Third, which of the four schools in section 2 would have prevented the Goshwara failure most cheaply, and which would merely have detected it sooner?

Yohal made two permanent changes and one refusal. The queue picker gained a denied state naming the role that grants access, and the migration tool now refuses to run without emitting a per-assignment loss report. She declined to ladder the other 33 queue surfaces, taking the four unoccupied states as evidence that a cheaper screen would do. Yamotra shipped the unknown state with its last-contact timestamp and overruled her platform lead, on the ground that a confident wrong number on 4,940 households is a warranty liability while an unhelpful true one is a support call.

13Going deeper

Table 4. Where to go next, and what each unlocks.
TopicWhy it matters next
Acceptance criteria and error casesMakes each state a criterion someone can fail.
Designing for errors and recoveryTakes failed and denied from named to recoverable.
PM artefacts: one-pager, PRD, spec, strategy docSettles which document the matrix belongs in.
Writing a one-pagerPuts Table 2's cost asymmetry where a sponsor reads it.
PRD structureGives the state set a home, not a whiteboard.
Customer narratives (Day 0 / Day N)Separates the empty state's two parents by construction.

exp20v2-req.edge.cases:
Edge Cases, States and Permissions

The screens nobody drew

1. Twelve days before release

On Thursday 22 October 2026, Manmeet Virdi, head of product at Ekpath, opened a spreadsheet nobody had asked her to build. Ekpath, a Ludhiana company, sells a billing and stock app to 18,400 distributors and wholesale kirana shops. On Tuesday 3 November it was due to release team access: an owner could invite a munim (the shop's accountant) and counter staff, each seeing different screens. Diwali fell on 8 November, and wholesalers restock hardest in the fortnight before it.

The beta had run for two weeks across 340 shops and had produced 85 support tickets. Mannat Verma, the QA lead, had tagged 51 of them, 60 per cent, with the same two words: "blank screen". None involved a wrong calculation. A counter employee opened Receivables and saw nothing, because the role lacked permission and the screen said nothing. A new owner saw an empty grey table. A shop in a basement godown lost signal mid-save, and the Save button spun until the owner force-closed the app.

The specification held fourteen acceptance criteria, every one describing an owner, online, with data, doing the right thing. Manmeet had three options: ship on 3 November, ship on 17 November, or ship on time and patch. At the beta's rate of 85 tickets per 340 shops, 0.25 per shop, full adoption at that rate would mean 4,600 tickets, arriving at a support desk of nine people led by Mohinder Vasdev in the busiest fortnight of the year. The question on her spreadsheet was narrower than any of the three options: how many distinct conditions did the Receivables screen have, and how many had anyone decided?

2. The idea: a screen is a family of screens

A state is a distinct condition a screen can be in, and each state needs its own answer to three questions: what does the person see, what can they do, and how do they leave. A designer's mock-up usually shows one state, the pleasant one, with data present, signal strong and the viewer fully authorised. A real screen is a function of at least four inputs: the condition of the data, the condition of the connection, who is looking, and what they have done before.

The vocabulary comes from two older fields. David Harel's 1987 statecharts gave engineers a way to draw every condition a system can occupy and every transition between them. Role-based access control, set out by David Ferraiolo and Richard Kuhn at the US standards body NIST in 1992, tied what a person may do to a role rather than to an individual. Product teams later merged the two ideas into a checklist: empty, loading, error, offline, first-run, and admin or restricted views.

"Edge case" is a misleading label. The empty state is the centre of the experience for every new customer, once. The sentence Manmeet could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib: we have specified the room with the lights on, and our users spend their first minute in the others. The sentence is useful because it moves the argument away from taste. Nobody can claim that a new owner's first screen is unimportant; it is the only screen that owner is certain to see.

3. How it works: enumerate, prune, collapse, decide

The method has six steps. First, name the dimensions that change what the screen shows. Second, list each dimension's values and multiply them; the product is the raw grid. Third, prune combinations that cannot occur. Fourth, collapse combinations that deserve an identical response. Fifth, give every surviving state a content, an action and an exit. Sixth, write each as an acceptance criterion, so that QA can test it and nobody must remember it. An acceptance criterion is a plain statement of behaviour that is either met or not, such as "a staff user opening Receivables sees a message naming the owner as the person who can grant access."

Two steps are usually left implicit. Pruning and collapsing are judgements, and someone must be named as accountable for them; otherwise engineering prunes silently to save effort and product collapses silently to save design. And the exit is the step most often forgotten: a state with a message but no way out, such as an error with no retry, is a dead end rather than a state.

Figure 1 shows the running example. The role check precedes the load, which is why a counter employee never reaches the data at all. From Loading, the screen leaves in one of three directions, and only one of them is the picture in the mock-up. Error returns to Loading by retry. Empty reaches Populated when the first record is saved, and Populated drops to Offline when signal is lost. Count the arrows: each one is an acceptance criterion, and most of them had never been written.

4. A worked example, line by line

Manmeet listed four dimensions for Receivables, the screen of unpaid customer invoices, and multiplied them.

DimensionValuesCount
Dataempty, loading, populated, error4
Connectiononline, offline2
Roleowner, accountant, staff3
Historyfirst-run, returning2
Raw grid4 × 2 × 3 × 248

She pruned two impossibilities. A first-run user cannot see populated data: 2 connection values × 3 roles = 6 combinations, leaving 42. And an offline screen has no loading state, because with no connection nothing is in flight: 2 histories × 3 roles = 6 more, leaving 36. The two rules do not overlap, since no row can be both populated and loading. Each role therefore holds 12 states (36 ÷ 3).

Then she collapsed. Staff may not see receivables at all, so their 12 states become one Denied screen: 36 − 12 + 1 = 25. Owner and accountant stay separate, because the accountant lacks a write-off button, which is a difference in permission, not in state. Section 1 described all fourteen criteria as owner, online, with data: in this grid that is one cell, owner, online, populated, returning. The criteria covered 1 of the 25 states, 4 per cent, leaving 24 unspecified.

Now change one input. Suppose the company lets staff view receivables read-only. Nothing collapses, and the total stays 36: eleven more states than the 25 above, and each of staff's 12 now needs writing. Alternatively suppose Ekpath declares the app online-only. The grid falls to 4 × 1 × 3 × 2 = 24; pruning first-run with data removes 3, leaving 21; collapsing staff's 7 gives 21 − 7 + 1 = 15. A single product decision, offline support, moved the specification burden from 25 states to 15, which is why it belongs in the product strategy and not in an engineer's afternoon.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

A state is not an error

Errors are one data value among four. Loading, empty and denied are not failures, yet teams that equate "states" with "errors" write a single generic message and consider the work done.

Empty is at least three states

A shop with no invoices ever, a filter that matches nothing and a list the user just cleared all show an empty table, but they need different words and different next steps. The first teaches, the second offers to widen the filter, the third confirms.

Hide, disable or explain

A permission can remove a control, grey it, or leave it live and refuse on click. Removing suits actions the role should never contemplate; greying with a reason suits actions the role could be granted. Silence suits nothing, which was the beta's blank screen.

Offline is not slow, and slow is not failed

Offline means no connection at all; slow means a connection that may deliver; failed means a request returned an error. Each calls for different behaviour: queue the work, show progress, offer retry. Conflating them produces the endless spinner.

Permission is not security

Hiding a button is a courtesy to the user. Enforcement belongs on the server, and engineering owns it. Product's job is the experience of being refused, which is a separate specification.

One person, several roles

At a small shop the owner is often also the counter clerk and the accountant. A role describes a set of permissions, not a human being, so the grid must be tested for people who hold two roles at once, and for the day an owner demotes herself.

The method cannot rank the states

Twenty-five states are not equally important. Enumeration finds them; only usage data says how many people stand in each. A newcomer should ask, before relying on the grid, which dimensions were left out. Any one of language, device or subscription status could have doubled it.

6. How it differs by product and by stage

In consumer products, first-run and empty states dominate, because the first session decides retention and every user starts with no data. In B2B products such as Ekpath, permissions and admin views dominate: an owner, an accountant and a clerk share one account but not one screen, and a missing admin state leaves the buyer unable to onboard colleagues. In marketplaces, every state doubles because each side sees its own: a seller with no listings and a buyer with no results are different empties, and each side may be forbidden to see the other's data.

Stage matters as much. An early-stage company with three engineers cannot specify 25 states for every screen; it should cover first-run, error and denied on the two or three screens that carry revenue, and accept the rest. A large company has the opposite problem: many teams, inconsistent empty and error screens, and permission rules that drift. Its answer is shared components and a single permission matrix, audited. In both cases the arithmetic of Figure 2 applies, and only the number of screens changes.

7. Common mistakes

The generic error message

Symptom: tickets that say "it didn't work", and users who tap Save repeatedly. Misunderstanding: an error is a message, rather than a state with an exit. Cheapest diagnostic: switch on aeroplane mode and try to finish the main task.

The vanished feature

Symptom: lower-role users asking the owner where a screen went. Misunderstanding: that permission is only a security matter. Diagnostic: sign in as the lowest role and open every menu.

Testing only with data

Symptom: new-customer drop-off on day one while seasoned users are content, because every tester's account was already full. Misunderstanding: that a populated test account represents a user. Diagnostic: create a fresh account and photograph each screen before adding anything.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of this decision looks undramatic. Before the build began, the team would have listed Receivables' 25 states in one sheet, with an owner for each prune and collapse. Each state would carry words, an action and an exit; the 24 uncovered states would already be criteria in the QA plan. Support would have seen the denied and first-run screens in a demonstration. The beta would then have produced tickets about features, not about nothing. Manmeet would still have found surprises, because no enumeration is complete, but they would have been surprises among states that already had owners, not among states nobody knew existed. The measure of success is modest: a support agent opening a complaint can name which of the 25 states the customer was standing in, and the fix is a line in a sheet rather than an investigation.

9. What Manmeet decided

She moved the release to Tuesday 17 November and said why in one paragraph to the executive team. The date cost two weeks of a promised feature; shipping into Diwali risked 4,600 tickets if every shop enabled it at the beta rate, a figure she presented as a scale marker, not a forecast. The fortnight after Diwali is slack for wholesalers and for support. She also ranked the 24 missing states by exposure: first-run empty, loading and error, which every shop meets on day one, were built first, and Mannat Verma's team re-tagged every beta ticket against the 25-state sheet, so the next beta could be read against a baseline.

What to learn next is designing for errors and recovery, because this page gave each error state an exit and left unanswered what the exit should say, how often to retry and what to do with work that cannot be saved.

Two questions to sit with. For a screen you own, which of its states have you yourself seen in the last month? And where does your product treat a lack of permission as a lack of existence, and who pays for that?
case20v1-req.edge.cases:
Tikaana Technologies: The Dues Release

1. Opening

At 7:40 pm on Monday, 19 October 2026, Ekroop Laroia sat alone in Tikaana Technologies' Indiranagar office in Bengaluru with a staging build of Dues 2.0 open on her phone. She had tapped through it six times, and it had worked every time. The feature lets residents of a housing society pay monthly maintenance by UPI and lets the treasurer see who has paid. It was due to reach residents with the November invoices on Sunday, 1 November, a week before Diwali.

Ekroop, Tikaana's head of product, had until 6 pm on Wednesday, 21 October to tell the Pune engineering team what to build for the store-build freeze at 6 pm on 28 October. She had a customer-success report from Singapore she had not finished reading, and a message from the designer in Berlin that began: "Before you decide, may I show you the states we never drew?"

2. Company background

Tikaana was founded in 2019 by two former residents' welfare association volunteers. Its app serves gated communities: guards approve visitors from a tablet, residents receive notices and raise complaints, and committees keep records. By October 2026 it served 1,850 societies in eleven cities, covering 4,20,000 homes at a subscription of ₹10 per home per month, or ₹5.04 crore a year. Of its 142 employees, most sit in Bengaluru and Pune, with customer success in Singapore, design in Berlin, an analytics group in Toronto and a sales head in New Jersey who works with builders' associations.

The category is crowded. MyGate and NoBrokerHood are the best-known names, Apna Complex and regional apps compete society by society, and many committees still collect maintenance by cheque, bank transfer and a WhatsApp group. UPI, run by NPCI, has made collection by app plausible: nearly every resident holds PhonePe, Paytm or another UPI app, and Tikaana routes payments through Razorpay. The society's committee chooses the vendor, so the treasurer is the buyer and the resident is the user whose patience sets the app-store rating.

Dues 2.0 was Tikaana's first direct revenue from payments: a convenience fee of ₹6 per home per month, billed to the society for each home that pays through the app.

3. The situation

The Dues 2.0 requirements document ran to eleven pages and described one journey: the invoice arrives, the resident taps Pay, the UPI app opens, the payment succeeds, a receipt appears, and the treasurer's list shows Paid. Its acceptance criteria covered that journey. Sixty-one societies had already circulated notices telling residents to pay through the app from 1 November.

In September, 38 societies with 11,400 homes had run Dues 2.0 as a beta. Of those homes, 6,840 (60 per cent) paid through the app. Within 30 days of the invoice the support queue received 684 tickets, 6.0 for every 100 homes. An analyst in Toronto coded them overnight; Exhibit 2 shows the result. At a blended ₹180 a ticket, the beta cost ₹1.23 lakh in support time.

Ekam Lohtia in Singapore, whose 14-agent team normally closes 3,100 tickets a month, had applied the beta ratio to all 4,20,000 homes (Exhibit 3). His team starts at 9 am Singapore time, 6:30 am in Bengaluru, so his report had been waiting since morning. Edhant Langeh in Pune had walked each role's flow with Eshpreet Lalli, the designer in Berlin, who works three and a half hours behind India until 25 October; their inventory is Exhibit 1. Four Pune engineers were free for Dues 2.0, as the rest were committed to consent screens required under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. Tikaana also keeps a festive change freeze from 5 to 15 November, and Diwali falls on 8 November (Figure 1).

Figure 1. Decision calendar, 2026 (IST). Each tick sits at the start of its day; scale 30 px per day from 19 October.

4. The people

Edhant Langeh, engineering manager, Pune. Twelve years in payments software. He wants a scope he can estimate and defend, and a team that is not working through the Diwali week. He prices each state he has to build at 1.5 engineer-days, including testing, and a day at ₹10,000. "Tell me the number of screens," he says, "and I will tell you the date."

Eshpreet Lalli, senior product designer, Berlin. She joined Tikaana from a Delhi design studio in 2023 and wants every state drawn before it is built. Her files hold ten complete frames against what she calls a hundred honest questions. "A blank screen is also a design," she wrote. "We just chose it by accident."

Ekam Lohtia, customer-success lead, Singapore. He answers to the societies' treasurers as well as the residents and has the company's longest memory of what an unclear screen costs in calls. He wants no launch that his team learns about from the queue. He also knows the sales head in New Jersey has promised the 61 societies a 1 November start.

Ekroop, the fourth person, holds the decision and the target: Dues 2.0 was meant to open Tikaana's second revenue line by year-end.

5. Exhibits

6. The options

Option A: ship as built. The staging build goes to all 1,850 societies on 1 November, with the figures in Exhibit 3 assuming every society enables it. No engineering time is spent, the 61 circulars are honoured, and the revenue line opens on schedule. The 26 identified states not yet built stay unbuilt.

Option B: build every missing state and ship after Diwali. Edhant's four engineers build all 26 states from 22 October, 9.75 working days, which finishes on Wednesday, 4 November. That misses the freeze and the festive change freeze, so the release goes out on 16 November, ahead of the December cycle. It costs 39 engineer-days, ₹3.90 lakh. No November revenue is earned.

Option C: build the eleven states for residents and treasurers, and ship to a cohort. The engineers build 11 of the 26 states by the freeze. That is 16.5 engineer-days, ₹1.65 lakh, finishing on the morning of 28 October. Dues 2.0 goes live on 1 November to 100 societies, the 61 that circulated notices plus 39 others, behind a switch the other societies cannot see. The cohort is sized at 22,700 homes, the base-wide average of 227 per society. The other 15 states stay unbuilt.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Map each cause in Exhibit 2 to a type of state: empty, loading, error, offline, first-time or permission. What does the pattern say about how Dues 2.0 was specified?
  2. Using Exhibit 3, what does each option cost and what does it forgo in the November cycle? Which figures would you trust least?
  3. With 26 states unbuilt and capacity for 11 before 28 October, how should Ekroop choose which 11?
  4. What should Ekroop tell Edhant on Wednesday, and what evidence after 1 November would make her change course?

8. A note for the learner

Edge cases are acceptance criteria for the states a happy-path specification leaves out: empty, loading, error, offline, first-time and the variants that depend on who is asking. Used as a lens, the topic turns the decision from "is the feature ready?" into "which people reach which states, and what happens to them there?". A well-reasoned answer inventories states by role, ties each to evidence of exposure, sequences the work because states do not cost the same, and limits how many users an unhandled state can reach.

One defensible path is Option C. In the beta, the payment, spinner and blank-screen causes account for 468 of 684 tickets, 68 per cent, and sit with resident-facing states Edhant can build before the freeze, together with two treasurer states. Ticket causes are not the same as states, so mapping them is a judgement; the cohort is therefore a way of testing it. At the beta rate, 22,700 homes would generate 1,362 tickets, 44 per cent of the 3,100 Ekam's team normally closes in a month, whereas a full launch with every society enabled would generate 25,200, about eight times that. Expansion would follow cohort by cohort, only while tickets stay below 6.0 per 100 homes, with role-change states built next. The path gives up most of the steady-state fee revenue in November, and Ekroop would pay for it with a plain message to the societies outside the cohort.
